Rugged tablet for Okappy

Okappy is job management and workforce software from Okappy Ltd, a UK company whose Google Play developer details give a London address. The vendor's Play listing describes it as workforce management and scheduling for plumbing, drainage and electrical contractors, facilities managers, councils and any company with employees or subcontractors working at different locations, and says it is ideal for companies with 5 to 250 employees or subcontractors. It is built around a network: customers can create jobs and forward them to you, and you can allocate jobs to your own engineers and to subcontractors. The office runs the jobs dashboard in a web browser; engineers view and update their jobs in the Okappy mobile app for Android or iOS.

The app is where the site work happens. The Play listing says engineers can view and update jobs assigned to them, see the location of colleagues, message them, add signatures, attach pictures, videos and documents, fill in tailored job sheets and checksheets, and get directions to the next job. Invoicing and reporting are marked web only. The vendor's features page says the app is optimised for poor or no network and sends updates when it next has signal, and its support article on photos and signatures says the engineer or customer signs with a finger or stylus on the device. That is a device that gets handed across a doorstep for a signature, rides in a van between jobs and comes out in the rain, which is where a consumer tablet with no sealing or drop rating tends to fail first.

This page sets out what Okappy publishes about the devices its app runs on, which Tuga rugged devices meet those published requirements, where the Windows tablet fits (the web dashboard in a browser) and where it does not, and how a UK contractor can buy one unit to try before kitting out a team.

Requirements

What Okappy needs from a device

Each item below comes from Okappy Ltd's own listing or documentation, with the source linked.

  • Android: Google Play lists Android 7.0 or later; the vendor's own page says Marshmallow and above

    The vendor's System requirements support article (published May 2017, last modified August 2022) says it supports Android v23 (Marshmallow) and above, which reads as API level 23, or Android 6.0, and asks users to upgrade the operating system before use. The Google Play listing checked on 19 October 2026 gives a minimum API level of 24, which is Android 7.0, so the Play figure is the one that decides whether the app will install. For Apple devices the same article says iOS 8.1 or above on an iPhone 5s or iPad 2 or later, while the App Store listing now asks for iOS 17.6 or later. No RAM or storage figure is published for phones or tablets. Source: okappy.com

  • Android app from Google Play, with a Phone device chip only

    The Android app is published on Google Play as Okappy - workforce management (package com.okappy.okappy, developer Okappy, with OKAPPY LTD. and a London address under the developer details). When checked on 19 October 2026 the listing showed version 3.0.60, updated 8 October 2026, a minimum API level of 24 (Android 7.0), a target API level of 36 and more than 5,000 downloads. The listing carried a device chip for Phone only; no Tablet or Chromebook chip was shown. The listing text nonetheless says you can manage your business from your tablet, phone or desktop computer, and the vendor's features page says its native apps work on most mobile devices from tablets to mobile phones, so expect a phone-style layout on a tablet rather than one designed for the larger screen. Source: play.google.com

  • Poor or no network: the app queues updates and sends them when it next has signal

    The vendor's mobile app features page says the app is optimised for poor or no network, that it is easy for engineers to update their work even with poor network, and that the app will send the updates when it next has network. The App Store version history adds that checksheets saved in memory load better in low-connectivity areas. The vendor does not publish how much job data is held on the device or whether a job can be opened for the first time without signal, and its photo troubleshooting article says queued images wait for the operating system to pick a time to upload based on network, power and other factors, with a recommendation to keep the app open on a good connection, ideally Wi-Fi. Source: okappy.com

  • Photos and videos through the device camera, and signatures by finger or stylus

    The support article on taking photos and capturing signatures says that on Android the app opens your camera app to take a photo or video, and that a signature is taken using your finger or stylus, then saved and named. The job management page says client signatures are captured on site using your touch screen device and presented in the final job sheet, and the features page says signatures can be made mandatory so a job cannot be completed until one is taken. The troubleshooting article asks Android users to keep the Camera and Storage permissions on, to keep documents under 10MB, and notes that power saving mode can slow uploads. Source: okappy.com

  • Job sheets and checksheets filled in on the app

    The vendor's support article on updating a job describes the engineer's flow on an iOS or Android device: any daily checksheet appears first, a risk assessment checksheet can be set to appear before the job is marked on site, the work done sheet follows the job template, and a closing checksheet such as customer feedback can follow that. Custom checksheets offer small, medium and large text fields, a numeric field, a rating field, a Yes/No field and a dropdown with custom options. A signature, image, video or document can be added at any stage from the Okappy icon or the + button. The vendor publishes no screen-size guidance for these forms. Source: okappy.com

  • GPS tracking with four settings, and the vendor's note that sending locations uses power

    The Mobile GPS tracking options article lists four ways to track devices: always track, track for a period of time, save the location and time stamp when updating jobs, or turn tracking off. It says sending locations uses power and recommends sending the location only with job updates if you want to save battery. The Radar tab in the web dashboard shows the latest location of all engineers. The vendor publishes no location accuracy or GNSS hardware requirement, and the Play listing notes the app shares location. Source: okappy.com

  • Windows: no Windows app, web dashboard in a current browser, with a recommended desktop specification

    The System requirements article says Okappy is web based and works across all operating systems, with a strong suggestion to run the latest Windows version. It recommends the latest Chrome, Safari, Microsoft Edge or Firefox and, because of TLS 1.3, does not support Internet Explorer, Chrome 69 and below, Edge 78 and below, Firefox 62 and below or Safari 12.1 and below. For desktops and laptops it recommends a minimum of 8GB of RAM, an Intel Core i5 processor or equivalent, 500GB of storage (noting Okappy is cloud based and does not need much storage itself) and a display of 21 inches or above for optimal viewing. The Play listing marks invoicing and reporting as web only. No barcode, QR or NFC scanning is documented anywhere in the vendor's help centre or listings. Source: okappy.com

Worth knowing. Okappy has no Windows app, so the Tuga W10 only runs the web dashboard in a browser. The engineer features the vendor documents (camera photos, finger or stylus signatures, checksheets, queued updates in poor signal and the Radar location sharing) are in the mobile app, so a W10 suits a site office or workshop desk, not an engineer on site, and it sits below the vendor's recommended desktop processor, storage and display size even though it meets the 8GB RAM minimum. On the Android side, the vendor's two published Android figures do not agree: its System requirements article (last modified 2022) says Marshmallow and above, while Google Play says Android 7.0; both are far below the Android 12, 14 and 15 on the A8, A10 and A6, so the gap does not change the answer. The Play listing carries a Phone device chip only, so expect a phone layout on a tablet. The vendor publishes no RAM, storage or screen-size figure for mobile devices, no barcode, QR or NFC support, and no location accuracy requirement, so the A6's Zebra 2D scan engine and the NFC radio on the A10, A8 and A6 should not be treated as Okappy features. The vendor's statements on offline working describe queued updates being sent when signal returns; it does not publish what is held on the device for first use without signal.
Setting up

Getting Okappy running

  1. Ask your Okappy administrator to add the engineer as a user in your Okappy account, and to set up the job sheet template and any daily, risk assessment, work done or closing checksheets you want to appear on the app.
  2. On the Tuga A8, A10 or A6, open Google Play and install Okappy - workforce management (package com.okappy.okappy, developer Okappy), then sign in with the engineer's details.
  3. When the app asks, allow the Camera and Storage permissions, which the vendor says are required for images to upload to jobs, and allow location access if your business uses the Radar map.
  4. In the web dashboard, pick the tracking setting that suits you: always track, track for a period, save the location only when a job is updated, or off. The vendor says sending locations uses power and suggests the job update option if you want to save battery.
  5. Before the first job in a poor signal area, open the app on a good connection so the engineer's jobs and checksheets are on the device. The vendor says updates made with no network are sent when the app next has signal, but publishes no detail on what is held for first use offline, so test a job in a known dead spot.
  6. Run a test job end to end: mark on site, take a photo, fill in the work done sheet, capture a signature with a finger or the stylus, and complete the job. Check the photo arrives on the dashboard; the vendor's troubleshooting article says a stuck image blocks the queue behind it and that resetting the app clears it.
  7. On a Tuga W10, open okappy.com in Edge or Chrome and keep the browser updated. Use it for the dashboard, invoicing and reporting; it will not run the mobile app.
  8. For the A8 and A10, fit the vehicle mounting dock in the van; for the A10 and W10, add the charging dock where devices live overnight; for the A6, add the belt holster. Fit the tempered glass screen protector before the device goes out.

Questions

Okappy on a Tuga device

Okappy's Google Play listing gives a minimum API level of 24, which is Android 7.0, and the vendor's own System requirements article says Marshmallow and above. The Tuga A8 runs Android 12 with Google Play, so it meets both, and so do the A10 (Android 14) and the A6 (Android 15). Okappy publishes no RAM or storage figure for phones or tablets, so the A8's 6GB, the A10's 8GB and the A6's 4GB cannot be checked against a vendor number. We do not describe any device as certified or tested by Okappy; these are the vendor's published requirements set against the device specifications, so try the app on one unit before buying for a team.

Partly, according to the vendor. Its features page says the app is optimised for poor or no network, that engineers can update their work with poor network, and that the app sends the updates when it next has network. It does not publish what is stored on the device for use before signal returns, so get the engineer's jobs onto the device on a good connection first. Queued photos wait for the operating system to pick an upload time, and the vendor recommends keeping the app open on a good connection, ideally Wi-Fi. The A8, A10 and A6 all have dual SIM 4G so a second network can cover a weak one. A Tuga W10 only runs the web dashboard, which the vendor does not describe as working offline.

When we checked Google Play on 19 October 2026 the Okappy listing carried a device chip for Phone only, with no Tablet chip. The vendor's own text says you can manage your business from your tablet, phone or desktop, its features page says the native apps work on most mobile devices from tablets to mobile phones, and its support article on adding jobs is written for iPad. Google Play normally still allows a phone app to install on an Android tablet, but the layout may be the phone one scaled up. That is one reason the 8 inch A8 is our first choice over the 10.1 inch A10, and why a single trial unit is worth running before a fleet order.

No scanning of any kind is documented. We found no barcode, QR code or NFC feature in Okappy's Google Play listing, App Store listing, help centre or features pages. The Tuga A6 has a Zebra 2D scan engine and the A10, A8 and A6 all have NFC, but none of that is an Okappy input, so do not choose a device for Okappy on that basis. Photos go through the camera app, which on the A8, A10 and A6 is a 13MP rear camera with flash.

The A8 suits most Okappy users: job sheets, checksheets, photos and finger signatures fit on its 8 inch 1000 nit screen, the 8000mAh battery is removable for days with GPS tracking on, it docks in the van through its VESA mount points, and it costs £379. Choose the A10 at £449 if you work in the wet or expect drops on hard surfaces, because it is IP68 and MIL-STD-810H where the A8 is IP67 with no MIL-STD rating, or if you want the larger 10.1 inch 1920 x 1200 screen for long work done sheets and attached documents, remembering that the app is published for phones.
